catalog_quote: 2.2 Word-stress in KM is phonemic. In the vast majority of words it is on the penult. When the penult contains /ə/ or /A/ it always falls on the final syllable (unless this contains /ə/, in which case it is on the penult again). There are, however, a number of words with end-stress and another vowel in the penult; cf. the following minimal pairs: /'barat/ 'west' vs. /ba'rat/ 'heavy', /'batu/ 'stone' vs. /ba'tu/ 'correct', /'sisik/ 'fish-scale' vs. /si'sik/ 'kind of edible sea-snail', /'parut/ 'to rasp' vs. /pa'rut, pa'ru/ 'belly' /'badak/ 'rhinoceros' vs. /ba'dak/ 'powder'. Below I will indicate stress only when it falls unpredictably on the final syllable. [Steinhauer 1983:44] ... The loss of the schwa led to the development of phonemic stress. In Vehicular Malay, stress fell on the penultimate syllable, unless this syllable contained a schwa, in which case stress fell on the final syl…

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim on Steinhauer 1983 p.44 sec. 2.2 in the page scan we hold, and the Paauw 2009 corroboration is verbatim at the stated pages (453-454; also 103-104). (2) The classification rests on a 1983 professional grammar sketch; no reference grammar of Kupang Malay exists in Glottolog (4 descriptive refs, two sketches), so the sketch plus Paauw's dissertation was already close to the best available. (3) The one better source that exists — Culhane & Kaland 2025, an instrumental study of 9189 syllables from six speakers — was downloaded now and confirms that word stress is produced and that its position is penult by default with a lexical set of final-stress words (source-schwa penults, Dutch loans, historic compounds) including minimal pairs; this supports classification lexical, edge='right', two-syllable window. sources.quote: p.1: 'Kupang Malay has been described as having stress either on the penultimate or ultimate syllable of the word, with penultimate stress being more common [Jacob 2001; Steinhauer 1983]. sources.note: Only quantitative study of Kupang Malay stress; confirms that the penult/final lexical stress positions described by Steinhauer 1983 are acoustically real (duration, spectral tilt, vowel quality) and restates the distribution with a schwa-less 5-vowel inventory — should be added as a corroborating source to a record that currently rests on a 1983 sketch.

sources.citation: Jacob, June A. & Barbara Dix Grimes. 2006. Developing a role for Kupang Malay: the contemporary politics of an eastern Indonesian creole. Paper presented at the Tenth International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics (10-ICAL), Puerto Princesa City, Palawan, Philippines, 17-20 January 2006. 24 pp.

tone.quote: Kupang Malay has contrastive stress. The general rule is for stress to fall on the penultimate syllable of the word. However, for Malay or Dutch words that were stressed on the last syllable, final stress in maintained.
tone.locator: p.3, section II 'A linguistic overview of Kupang Malay', A.1 'Phonology', (a) 'Different stress patterns' (section I is 'The historical background of Kupang Malay')
